newsitem.title: USA: Florida community still simmers in riot's wake.
newsitem.headline: Florida community still simmers in riot's wake.

text.p: Black community leaders, saying they did not trust the local law-enforcement apparatus, called on Monday for an outside investigator to probe the cause of a night of violence in an inner-city neighbourhood last week.

Black leaders and law-enforcement officials argued over who should investigate the shooting of 18-year-old black motorist Tyron Lewis by white police officer James Knight that sparked the rioting Thursday evening. Knight had stopped Lewis for speeding.
Sevell Brown III, president of the local Southern Christian Leadership Conference chapter, said residents wanted an outside investigator.

"The state attorney's office has an ongoing strong relationship with the police department," he told Reuters. "Essentially, we have to deal with the perception of police impropriety, we must maintain the integrity of the investigation by having an independent prosecutor appointed by the governor."

Police reported 28 arson fires during some eight hours of rioting, which spread through predominantly black south St. Petersburg with word of Lewis's death. Hundreds of people threw rocks and bottles at police and motor vehicles and buildings were burned.
The city was calm all weekend and a state of emergency issued Friday was cancelled Sunday, a day earlier than anticipated, leaving community leaders to debate what should be done next.

In an interview with Reuters Monday, St. Petersburg Mayor David Fischer blamed the riot on "agitators" who had appealed to a larger number of disaffected youths. "We need to work on that crowd that follows the agitators," he said.

"We need to be able to give those young men better education, jobs, some hope, a destiny. But ironically, we recognised that we had a disaffected minority population some time ago. We even applied to have an Enterprize Zone but were turned down because we were too good and other communities needed them more."

Lilla Davis, a spokeswoman for the St. Petersburg police department, said the two officers involved in the shooting would be on administrative leave until several investigations that have been launched were completed.

In Washington officials said Friday the Federal Bureau of Investigation was launching an inquiry and a delegation from the U.S. Civil Rights Commission was due in the city to look at race relations. State Attorney Bernie McCabe was also leading an investigation into the shooting, as he does any such incident that results in a fatality.
McCabe said he had no idea how long he would take to reach a conclusion as to the correctness of the officers' actions.
Responding to black community leaders who said they were not ready to trust the state attorney's investigation, he told Reuters, "They (the SCLC) are just trying to stir up trouble."

SCLC leader Brown said: "The governor is accorded this power by our state constitution. It's actually built in for just this sort of occurrence. I'm astonished at (McCabe's) attitude. I call on the state attorney to take the moral high ground and take preventive measures to give us some positive resolution."

Brown said Lewis's funeral would not take place until Saturday because of the Oct. 31 Halloween celebrations, which in many U.S. cities lead to disturbances. Joseph Lowery, national president of the SCLC, was to delivery the eulogy.
